notes.definition: The reactivity series is a list of metals in order of their reactivity, from most to least reactive. The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions: the more easily a metal atom loses electrons, the more reactive the metal.
explanation: When metals react with other substances, the metal atoms lose their outer shell electrons and form positive ions. Some metals do this much more easily than others. The more readily a metal forms its positive ion, the more reactive it is. Arranging metals by how vigorously they react gives the reactivity series: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper, from most reactive to least reactive. The non-metals carbon and hydrogen are often included as reference points.

With cold water, the most reactive metals form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Potassium reacts very vigorously: it melts, whizzes around on the surface and the hydrogen burns with a lilac flame. Sodium melts into a ball and fizzes as it moves around. Lithium fizzes steadily and moves on the surface but does not melt. Calcium fizzes steadily and the water turns cloudy. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water, and zinc, iron and copper show no reaction. For example: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g).

With dilute acids, metals above hydrogen form a salt and hydrogen. Potassium, sodium and lithium react dangerously violently with acids, so these reactions are not done in school. Calcium reacts very vigorously and magnesium fizzes vigorously. Zinc fizzes steadily and iron produces only a few slow bubbles. Copper is below hydrogen in the series and does not react with dilute acids at all. The rate of bubbling is a simple way to compare reactivity, as long as the acid concentration, volume, temperature and the size of the metal pieces are kept the same.

A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its compounds. If an iron nail is placed in blue copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper: Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). A pink-brown coating of copper forms on the nail and the blue colour fades as pale green iron sulfate forms. If copper is placed in iron sulfate solution, nothing happens, because copper is less reactive than iron. Displacement reactions are exothermic, and the further apart the two metals are in the series, the larger the temperature rise.

You can deduce an order of reactivity from experimental results. In a displacement grid, the metal that displaces the most other metals is the most reactive, and the one that displaces none is the least reactive. With acids, faster bubbling or a bigger temperature rise means a more reactive metal. Carbon is placed between magnesium and zinc in the series, so metals below carbon can be extracted from their oxides by heating with carbon. Hydrogen is placed between iron and copper, so metals above hydrogen produce hydrogen gas with dilute acids.
keyFacts: Order of reactivity (most to least): potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper.
When metals react, their atoms lose electrons to form positive ions.
The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions.
Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen (for the most reactive metals).
Metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen (for metals above hydrogen).
Copper does not react with water or with dilute acids.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound, for example Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
Carbon and hydrogen are included in the series as reference points.
Only reactions with water at room temperature are needed, not reactions with steam.

keyTerms.definition: A list of metals arranged in order of how vigorously they react, from most reactive to least reactive.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.
An ion formed when an atom loses electrons, such as Na⁺ or Mg²⁺. Metals form positive ions.
A compound such as sodium hydroxide (NaOH) formed, along with hydrogen, when a reactive metal reacts with water.
A compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal, such as magnesium chloride.
Describes a substance that takes part in chemical reactions readily and vigorously.

workedExamples.title: Deducing an order from a displacement grid
workedExamples.question: Three metals P, Q and R are added to solutions of each other's sulfates. P displaces Q and R. Q displaces R but not P. R displaces neither P nor Q. Put the metals in order of reactivity.
steps: A metal can only displace a less reactive metal.
P displaces both others, so P is the most reactive.
Q displaces R only, so Q is more reactive than R but less reactive than P.
R displaces nothing, so R is the least reactive.
workedExamples.answer: P (most reactive), then Q, then R (least reactive).

workedExamples.title: Using temperature rise data
workedExamples.question: Equal masses of magnesium, zinc and iron powder were added to 25 cm³ portions of the same copper sulfate solution. The temperature rises were: magnesium 34.5 °C, zinc 17.0 °C, iron 8.5 °C. Use the results to place the four metals (including copper) in order of reactivity.
steps: Each metal displaced copper, so all three are more reactive than copper.
The larger the temperature rise, the more energy is released and the more reactive the metal compared with copper.
Magnesium gave the biggest rise, then zinc, then iron.
Copper is the least reactive because it was displaced by all three.

workedExamples.title: Writing the equation for a reaction with water
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for calcium reacting with water to form calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, and hydrogen.
steps: Word equation: calcium + water → calcium hydroxide + hydrogen.
Count: right side has 2 O and 4 H, so 2H₂O are needed on the left.
Add state symbols: calcium is solid, water liquid, calcium hydroxide aqueous, hydrogen gas.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a less reactive metal can displace a more reactive one if you leave it long enough.
misconceptions.right: Displacement only happens when the metal added is more reactive than the metal in the compound. Copper in iron sulfate solution will never react.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals react with water to form a metal oxide and hydrogen.
misconceptions.right: With cold water, reactive metals form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, for example sodium hydroxide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon and hydrogen are metals because they appear in the reactivity series.
misconceptions.right: Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals. They are included as reference points to compare with the metals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all metals react with acids.
misconceptions.right: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids. Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.

realWorld: Copper is used for water pipes and hot water tanks because it does not react with water.
Potassium and sodium are stored under oil to stop them reacting with water vapour and oxygen in the air.
Gold and copper have been used for coins and jewellery for thousands of years because they are unreactive and do not corrode easily.
Displacement of copper by scrap iron is used to recover copper from solutions of copper compounds.
examTips: Learn the order with a mnemonic, for example 'Please Send Lions, Cats, Monkeys And Cute Zebras Into Hot Countries' (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu).
When asked to explain displacement, compare the two metals: 'iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from copper sulfate'.
For a displacement grid, count how many reactions each metal gives: most reactions = most reactive.
Give observations, not products, when asked what you would see: 'fizzing' or 'bubbles', not 'hydrogen is made'.
When comparing metals with acid, mention a fair test: same acid concentration and volume, same mass and surface area of metal, same temperature.
summary: The reactivity series lists metals from most to least reactive: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu.
Reactivity depends on how easily a metal forms positive ions.
Reactive metals + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen.
Metals above hydrogen + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compounds.
Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points.

flashcards.front: Order of reactivity for K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu
flashcards.back: Potassium > sodium > lithium > calcium > magnesium > zinc > iron > copper.

flashcards.front: What is the reactivity of a metal related to?
flashcards.back: Its tendency to form positive ions (lose electrons).

flashcards.front: Products when a reactive metal reacts with water
Products when a metal reacts with a dilute acid
Describe the reaction of sodium with water.
flashcards.back: Melts into a ball, fizzes, moves around on the surface, gets smaller and disappears.

flashcards.front: Describe the reaction of potassium with water.
flashcards.back: Very vigorous: melts, moves quickly, hydrogen burns with a lilac flame, may spark.

flashcards.front: How does copper react with water and dilute acids?
flashcards.back: It does not react with either.
A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.

flashcards.front: What do you see when iron is put in copper sulfate solution?
flashcards.back: Pink-brown copper coats the iron and the blue solution fades to pale green.

flashcards.front: Where is carbon in the reactivity series and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Between magnesium (and aluminium) and zinc. Metals below carbon can be extracted by heating with carbon.

flashcards.front: Where is hydrogen in the reactivity series and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Between iron and copper. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to give hydrogen.

questions.question: Which of these metals is the most reactive?
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium
questions.explanation: Potassium is at the top of the reactivity series. Magnesium is fairly reactive, zinc less so, and copper is the least reactive of these.

questions.question: Which gas is produced when lithium reacts with water?
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen
questions.explanation: Reactive metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Oxygen is not released: the oxygen stays in the hydroxide.

questions.question: Which metal does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper
questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids. Iron reacts slowly but it does react.

questions.question: What are the products when calcium reacts with water?
markScheme: 1 mark: calcium hydroxide and hydrogen
questions.explanation: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. The cloudiness seen is calcium hydroxide, which is only slightly soluble.

questions.question:
Complete the sentence.
The reactivity of a metal is related to ____________.
options: its tendency to form positive ions
its tendency to form negative ions
markScheme: 1 mark: its tendency to form positive ions
questions.explanation: Metals react by losing electrons to form positive ions. The more easily this happens, the more reactive the metal. Metals do not form negative ions.

questions.question: Which mixture would react?
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium and copper sulfate solution
questions.explanation: Displacement only happens if the solid metal is more reactive than the metal in the compound. Magnesium is more reactive than copper. In the other mixtures the solid metal is less reactive.

questions.question: Why is carbon often included in the reactivity series?
options: Carbon shows which metals react with acids
It shows which metal oxides can be reduced by heating with carbon
markScheme: 1 mark: it shows which metals can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon
questions.explanation: Carbon is a non-metal used as a reference point. Metals below carbon can be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon. Hydrogen, not carbon, is the reference point for reactions with acids.

questions.question: A small piece of lithium is added to a trough of cold water. Which observation is correct?
options: It burns with a lilac flame
It fizzes steadily and moves on the surface without melting
It melts into a ball and catches fire
markScheme: 1 mark: it fizzes steadily and moves on the surface without melting
questions.explanation: Lithium is the least reactive of the three Group 1 metals in the series: it floats, fizzes and moves but does not melt. Sodium melts into a ball; potassium burns with a lilac flame.

questions.question:
A student added metals X, Y and Z to solutions of each other's sulfates.
Table 1 shows the results.
✓ = reaction    ✗ = no reaction
What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
markScheme: 1 mark: X, Y, Z
questions.explanation: X displaces both other metals (2 reactions), Y displaces one (Z), and Z displaces none. The metal with the most reactions is the most reactive.

questions.question: Potassium reacts more vigorously with water than lithium. Which statement best explains this?
options: Potassium atoms lose their outer electron more easily to form positive ions
Potassium atoms gain electrons more easily to form negative ions
Potassium has a higher melting point than lithium
Potassium forms a hydroxide but lithium forms an oxide
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium atoms lose their outer electron more easily (greater tendency to form positive ions)
questions.explanation: Reactivity is related to the tendency of a metal to form its positive ion. Both form hydroxides with water, and metals do not form negative ions.

questions.question:
A student added zinc powder to copper sulfate solution.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the temperature rise.
questions.explanation: Temperature rise = highest temperature − starting temperature = 34.0 − 20.5 = 13.5 °C.

questions.question:
A student repeated a displacement experiment three times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean temperature rise.
questions.explanation: Add the three values (36.3) and divide by the number of results (3): 36.3 ÷ 3 = 12.1 °C.

questions.question:
A piece of zinc reacted with dilute sulfuric acid.
45 cm³ of hydrogen was collected in 90 seconds.
Calculate the mean rate of hydrogen production.
Use the equation:
mean rate of reaction = volume of gas produced ÷ time taken
markScheme: 1 mark: 45 ÷ 90 = 0.5 cm³/s
questions.explanation: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 45 ÷ 90 = 0.5 cm³ per second. A faster rate with the same conditions would suggest a more reactive metal.

questions.question:
A student added magnesium powder and iron powder to separate samples of copper sulfate solution.
Table 1 shows the results.
How many times larger was the temperature rise with magnesium than with iron?
questions.explanation: 26.0 ÷ 6.5 = 4. Magnesium is much further above copper in the reactivity series than iron, so more energy is released.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with water.
Name the two products of the reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium hydroxide
1 mark: hydrogen
questions.explanation: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a small piece of sodium being added to a trough of cold water.
Describe two observations you would make.

markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: fizzes / bubbles; melts into a ball; floats / moves around on the surface; gets smaller and disappears
questions.explanation: Observations are what you see, so 'hydrogen is produced' would not score, but 'fizzing' does.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with water.
Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
Include state symbols.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae balanced: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
1 mark: correct state symbols (s), (l), (aq), (g)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is diatomic (H₂), so two NaOH must form, which needs two Na and two H₂O. Sodium hydroxide dissolves, so it is (aq).

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows an iron nail in blue copper sulfate solution.
The nail is left for an hour.
Describe what you would see.
Explain why this happens.

markScheme: 1 mark: pink-brown / orange-brown coating (of copper) on the nail
1 mark: blue colour of the solution fades / turns pale green
1 mark: iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution
questions.explanation: Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). The copper that forms coats the nail; the iron sulfate solution formed is pale green.

questions.question:
A piece of copper is placed in zinc sulfate solution.
There is no reaction.
Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: copper is less reactive than zinc
markScheme: 1 mark: copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc
questions.explanation: A metal can only displace a less reactive metal from its compound. Copper is below zinc in the reactivity series.

questions.question:
Magnesium is more reactive than zinc.
Explain why, in terms of ions.
acceptedAnswers: magnesium forms positive ions more easily
greater tendency to form positive ions
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium has a greater tendency to form (positive) ions / loses electrons more easily than zinc
questions.explanation: The reactivity of a metal is related to how readily it forms its positive ion. Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ more readily than zinc forms Zn²⁺.

questions.question: Suggest why potassium is never added to dilute acid in a school laboratory.
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction would be (dangerously) violent / explosive because potassium is very reactive
questions.explanation: Potassium already reacts very vigorously with water. With acid the reaction is even more violent and could explode.

questions.question:
A student compares the reactivity of magnesium, zinc and iron.
The student adds each metal to dilute hydrochloric acid and observes the bubbling.
Give two variables the student must keep the same.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: concentration of acid; volume of acid; type of acid; mass of metal; size / surface area of metal pieces (e.g. all powder or all granules); starting temperature
questions.explanation: Only the metal should change. Larger surface area, more concentrated acid or a higher temperature would all make the bubbling faster and could give a misleading order.

questions.question:
Zinc reacts with copper sulfate solution.
Write the word equation for the reaction.
acceptedAnswers: zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper
markScheme: 1 mark: zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper
questions.explanation: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it swaps places with copper in the compound.

questions.question:
A student is given samples of magnesium, zinc, iron and copper and some dilute sulfuric acid.
Plan an investigation to place the four metals in order of reactivity.
Your plan should describe how to make the test fair and how the results would be used.
markScheme: Indicative content: place the same volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of the same concentration of dilute sulfuric acid in four test tubes or boiling tubes; use the same mass and similar size / surface area of each metal (e.g. all granules or all powder); same starting temperature; add one metal to each tube; observe the rate of bubbling or measure the temperature rise with a thermometer, or collect gas in a gas syringe over a fixed time; more bubbles, faster gas collection or a larger temperature rise means a more reactive metal; expect magnesium most vigorous, then zinc, then iron (slow), and copper no reaction; repeat to check results; wear eye protection.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent plan with control of at least two variables, a clear measurement or observation, and explanation of how results give the order of reactivity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with some control of variables and some idea of how to compare reactivity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as add the metals to acid and watch, with little detail.
questions.explanation: A good plan changes only the metal, measures something that shows how fast or how strongly each metal reacts, and links a bigger effect to higher reactivity.

questions.question:
A student added four metals to solutions of metal sulfates.
Table 1 shows the results.
✓ = reaction    ✗ = no reaction
Deduce the order of reactivity of the four metals.
Explain how the results support your order.
markScheme: Indicative content: order magnesium > zinc > X > copper; a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound; magnesium displaces all three others (3 reactions) so it is most reactive; zinc displaces X and copper (2 reactions) but not magnesium; X displaces only copper (1 reaction); copper displaces none, so it is least reactive; X is less reactive than zinc because it does not displace zinc and zinc displaces it.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct order with clear reasoning using displacement for each metal.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): partly correct order or correct order with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Count the ticks for each metal: 3, 2, 1, 0. More displacements means more reactive. Comparing a pair directly (zinc and X) confirms the order.

questions.question:
Potassium, sodium and lithium all react with cold water.
Compare the reactions.
Explain the differences in terms of the tendency of each metal to form positive ions.
markScheme: Indicative content: all three float, fizz and produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen; lithium fizzes steadily and does not melt; sodium reacts faster and melts into a ball; potassium reacts most violently, melts and the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; order of reactivity potassium > sodium > lithium; potassium has the greatest tendency to lose its outer electron and form a positive ion (K⁺); lithium the least (Li⁺).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct comparison of all three reactions and a clear link between vigour of reaction and the tendency to form positive ions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct observations or a correct order, with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: The more easily a metal atom loses its outer electron, the more vigorously it reacts. All three give the same type of products; only the vigour changes.

questions.question:
A student tests metal M.
Table 1 shows the results.
Where does M fit in the reactivity series?

rows: M added to dilute hydrochloric acid
